cards.front: How does the T-cell receptor differ structurally from cytokine receptors that use JAK-STAT signalling?
cards.back: Its intracellular tail is only a few amino acids long with no enzyme, and unlike cytokine receptors its own chains do not even hold a kinase.
cards.why: Because its recognition chains lack both catalytic domains and bound kinases, partner chains must transmit the signal inside.
cards.quote: Unlike the cytokine receptors in JAK-STAT signalling, its own chains do not even hold a kinase.

cards.front: For most T cells, an antigen is a short peptide held in the groove of an {{c1::MHC protein}}, a display molecule on another cell.
cards.back: Surface display protein presenting short peptides to T-cell receptors.
cards.quote: for most T cells, a short peptide held in the groove of an MHC protein, a display molecule on another cell.
cards.section: One set of chains recognises, another set signals

cards.front: In a T-cell receptor complex, which chains recognise antigen and which partner chains carry the intracellular signalling tails?
cards.back: The alpha and beta chains recognise antigen via variable outer tips; the partner chains CD3 gamma, delta, epsilon, and zeta signal inside.
cards.why: The alpha and beta chains also require these partner chains to reach the cell surface.
cards.quote: The receptor travels with partner chains—CD3 gamma, delta and epsilon, plus zeta—which it needs to reach the surface.
cards.section: One set of chains recognises, another set signals

cards.front: The conserved partner-chain motif Y-x-x-(L or I), 6 to 8 residues, Y-x-x-(L or I) is called an {{c1::ITAM}}.
cards.back: Immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif.
cards.quote: The pattern is now called an ITAM (immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif).
cards.section: One set of chains recognises, another set signals

cards.front: One T-cell receptor complex carries {{c1::ten}} ITAMs: three on each of its two zeta tails and one on each of its four CD3 tails.
cards.back: Six ITAMs on the two zeta chains plus four on the four CD3 chains.
cards.quote: One T-cell receptor complex carries ten ITAMs: three on each of its two zeta tails and one on each of its four CD3 tails.
cards.section: One set of chains recognises, another set signals

cards.front: Irving and Weiss fused the outer and membrane-crossing regions of CD8 to the cytoplasmic zeta tail alone—creating a hybrid that recognised no antigen—and clustered it on T cells with an anti-CD8 antibody. What happened, and what did it prove?
cards.back: The T cells activated, proving that the cytoplasmic zeta tail alone is sufficient to trigger activation signals without the antigen-recognising chains.
cards.quote: Clustering the CD8–zeta hybrid set off activation signals (other laboratories reported similar hybrids that year). The zeta tail alone was enough to signal.
cards.section: One set of chains recognises, another set signals

cards.front: The Src-family tyrosine kinase {{c1::Lck}} is held to the inner membrane by fatty acid chains and phosphorylates ITAM tyrosines after receptor engagement.
cards.back: Already partly active at rest, with a share riding on CD4 or CD8.
cards.quote: The first film introduced the Src-family tyrosine kinase Lck (protein interaction modules), held to the inner membrane by fatty acid chains and already partly active at rest
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: In the leading model of T-cell receptor triggering, what happens to ITAM phosphorylation if the bulky phosphatase CD45 is prevented from being pushed out of the tight contact between two cells, and why?
cards.back: Phosphates fail to accumulate on engaged receptors, because CD45 stays in the contact zone and continues removing the phosphates that partly active Lck adds.
cards.why: How triggering works is still debated, but this model relies on physical exclusion of CD45.
cards.quote: In one leading model, pressing both cells close pushes bulky CD45 out of the contact so phosphates accumulate on engaged receptors; how triggering works is still debated.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Finding Lck attached to CD4 and CD8 in broken-open T cells showed association, not necessity. In a mutant T-cell line with intact receptors, a faulty Lck gene, and no calcium response, what experimental step proved Lck was required?
cards.back: Restoring an intact Lck gene to the mutant line and observing the calcium response return, which ruled out an unrelated defect elsewhere in the cell line.
cards.quote: Restoring an intact Lck gene to the mutant line and seeing the calcium response return, which ruled out an unrelated defect elsewhere in the line.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Why must both tyrosines of a single ITAM be phosphorylated before ZAP-70 binds tightly, and what does this requirement protect against?
cards.back: ZAP-70's two side-by-side SH2 domains are spaced to grip both phosphotyrosines at once, preventing a stray single phosphate from firing the T cell.
cards.quote: Once Lck phosphorylates both ITAM tyrosines, the tyrosine kinase ZAP-70 docks via two side-by-side SH2 domains (phosphotyrosine-binding modules) spaced to fit both marks.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Trace the activation steps in a T cell from doubly phosphorylated ITAMs to the membrane scaffold LAT.
cards.back: Docking on doubly phosphorylated ITAMs opens ZAP-70, Lck phosphorylates ZAP-70, and ZAP-70 phosphorylates LAT to create SH2 docking sites for downstream branches.
cards.quote: Docking opens ZAP-70, Lck phosphorylates it, and ZAP-70 phosphorylates LAT, a membrane scaffold (adaptors and scaffolds) whose phosphotyrosines become SH2 docking sites.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: In the calcium branch of T-cell signalling, phosphorylated PLC-gamma splits {{c1::PIP2}} into IP3 and DAG.
cards.back: IP3 mobilises calcium while DAG feeds the PKC and Ras branches.
cards.quote: PLC-gamma docks, is activated by phosphorylation, splits PIP2 into IP3 and DAG (PLC, IP3, DAG and PKC)
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: How does IP3 generated by PLC-gamma activate the transcription factor NFAT in a T cell?
cards.back: IP3 empties Ca²⁺ stores, store-operated channels sustain Ca²⁺, and calmodulin activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT so it can enter the nucleus.
cards.quote: IP3 empties Ca²⁺ stores; store-operated channels sustain Ca²⁺ (calcium signalling); calmodulin switches on the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT (the phosphorylation switch)
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: How does DAG generated by PLC-gamma contribute to both the PKC and Ras signalling branches in a T cell?
cards.back: DAG recruits PKC-theta to activate IκB kinase and NF-κB, and also activates RasGRP (alongside Grb2–SOS) to load Ras with GTP, driving Raf–MEK–ERK and AP-1.
cards.quote: DAG recruits PKC-theta, leading through a scaffold complex to IκB kinase (the NF-κB pathway)
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Which three transcription factors activated by the pathways leaving LAT converge on control regions of genes such as interleukin-2?
cards.back: NFAT (calcium branch), NF-κB (PKC branch), and AP-1 (Ras–ERK branch).
cards.why: Interleukin-2 is a cytokine that drives T-cell division through a JAK-STAT receptor.
cards.quote: NFAT, NF-κB and AP-1 meet on the control regions of genes such as interleukin-2, a cytokine driving T-cell division through a JAK-STAT receptor.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: The transplant drug cyclosporin inhibits calcineurin in a stimulated T cell. Which transcription factor stays out of the nucleus, what happens to the other two branches from LAT, and what happens to interleukin-2 activation?
cards.back: Interleukin-2 activation is sharply suppressed because NFAT remains phosphorylated in the cytosol; the PKC–NF-κB and Ras–ERK branches still run, but genes such as interleukin-2 need all three factors together.
cards.quote: Because genes such as interleukin-2 need all three factors together, blocking one branch sharply suppresses activation.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Suppose a mutation deletes one of the two SH2 domains of ZAP-70 in a T cell. What happens to LAT phosphorylation and the three downstream branches after receptor engagement, and why?
cards.back: LAT phosphorylation and the calcium, PKC, and Ras branches fail to fire efficiently, because ZAP-70 needs both side-by-side SH2 domains to bind doubly phosphorylated ITAMs tightly, open up, and phosphorylate LAT.
cards.quote: Tight binding needs both phosphates, preventing a stray phosphate from firing the cell.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: When a T-cell receptor is triggered with a light-activated peptide, LAT is phosphorylated within {{c1::4 seconds}} and intracellular calcium rises within 6 to 7 seconds.
cards.back: Early antigen-receptor signalling runs on a timescale of seconds.
cards.quote: Triggering the receptor with a light-activated peptide phosphorylated LAT within 4 seconds and raised calcium within 6 to 7 seconds (Huse and colleagues, 2007).
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Why does a T cell require a second signal and inhibitory brakes even though its antigen receptor can fire within seconds?
cards.back: Because T-cell receptors vary almost at random and some fit self peptides, extra checks and brakes are needed to prevent activation against self tissues.
cards.quote: because receptors vary almost at random and some fit self peptides, a T cell needs a second check before committing—and brakes to hold it back.
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: Suppose all tyrosines in the zeta-chain ITAMs of a T cell are mutated so Lck cannot phosphorylate them, while the zeta chains still assemble with intact CD3 chains at the cell surface. Predict how many functional ITAMs remain per receptor complex and whether ZAP-70 can still activate LAT.
cards.back: Four functional ITAMs remain per complex (down from 10, a 60% drop), so ZAP-70 can still dock on the four intact CD3 ITAMs and phosphorylate LAT, though with fewer docking sites. This rests on the rules that one TCR complex carries three ITAMs on each of two zeta tails and one on each of four CD3 tails, and that Lck phosphorylating both tyrosines of any ITAM allows ZAP-70 to dock, open, and phosphorylate LAT.
cards.quote: Docking opens ZAP-70, Lck phosphorylates it, and ZAP-70 phosphorylates LAT
cards.section: The first minute: Lck, ZAP-70 and three branches from LAT

cards.front: How does the CD28–B7 co-stimulatory signal tie naive T-cell activation to the presence of infection?
cards.back: A T cell meeting its antigen for the first time needs CD28 to bind B7 on the presenting cell, which displays far more B7 after detecting signs of infection.
cards.quote: CD28 must bind a B7 protein (B7-1 or B7-2) on the presenting cell, which displays far more B7 after detecting signs of infection.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: In classic experiments on cultured T cells, stimulating the antigen receptor without CD28 drove the cells into a lasting unresponsive state called {{c1::anergy}}.
cards.back: Signal one alone silences the T cell rather than activating it.
cards.quote: In the classic experiments on cultured T cells, signal one alone did worse than nothing: the cells entered a lasting unresponsive state called anergy.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: CD28 has no catalytic enzyme in its short tail; once phosphorylated, a tyrosine motif recruits {{c1::PI 3-kinase}} and Grb2.
cards.back: Phosphotyrosine docking transmits signal two inside the T cell.
cards.quote: CD28 has no enzyme either: once phosphorylated, a tyrosine motif in its short tail recruits PI 3-kinase (PI 3-kinase, Akt and insulin) and Grb2.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: Why is CTLA-4's competitive advantage over CD28 even wider on intact cells than predicted from isolated-protein binding affinities alone?
cards.back: On a cell, a CTLA-4 dimer grips two B7 molecules at once and physically pulls B7 off the presenting cell into the T cell to be destroyed.
cards.quote: a CTLA-4 dimer grips two B7 molecules at once and physically pulls B7 off the presenting cell into the T cell to be destroyed
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: For soluble B7-1 on isolated proteins, the dissociation constant Kd is near {{c1::0.4 µM}} for CTLA-4 versus 4 µM for CD28.
cards.back: CTLA-4 binds B7 roughly ten times more tightly than CD28.
cards.quote: the dissociation constant Kd (the free ligand concentration at which half the receptors are occupied) is near 0.4 µM for CTLA-4 versus 4 µM for CD28.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: For soluble B7-1 on isolated proteins, Kd is 4 µM for CD28 and 0.4 µM for CTLA-4. Using simple one-site binding, fraction bound = [L] / (Kd + [L]), about what percentage of each receptor is occupied when free B7-1 is 2.0 µM?
cards.why: Even well above CTLA-4's Kd, CTLA-4 captures about 2.5 times the fraction of bound sites as CD28.
cards.quote: Using simple one-site binding, where fraction bound = [L] / (Kd + [L]), suppose free B7-1 is 1.0 µM.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: With Kd = 4 µM for CD28 and Kd = 0.4 µM for CTLA-4 under simple one-site binding, fraction bound = [L] / (Kd + [L]), what free B7-1 concentration half-saturates CD28, and about what percentage of CTLA-4 is occupied at that same concentration?
cards.back: 4.0 µM free B7-1 half-saturates CD28 (since [L] = Kd = 4 µM). At 4.0 µM, CTLA-4 occupancy is 4.0 / (0.4 + 4.0) = 4.0 / 4.4 ≈ 0.909, or about 91%.
cards.quote: On isolated proteins, CTLA-4 binds B7 roughly ten times more tightly than CD28
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: Mice lacking CTLA-4 died within weeks of birth with unchecked lymphocyte proliferation, and deleting CTLA-4 solely from regulatory T cells also caused fatal autoimmunity. What do these two knockout experiments establish?
cards.back: CTLA-4 is essential in vivo to restrain lymphocyte proliferation and prevent attack on self tissues, and regulatory T cells rely heavily on CTLA-4 to maintain that restraint.
cards.quote: deleting CTLA-4 from regulatory T cells alone caused fatal autoimmunity (an immune attack on the body's own tissues) in mice (Shimon Sakaguchi's laboratory, 2008).
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: When PD-L1 binds PD-1 on an activated T cell, phosphorylation of a tyrosine in PD-1's {{c1::ITSM}} recruits the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2.
cards.back: Immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motif—a phosphatase-docking site, not an ITAM.
cards.quote: the main one, in the ITSM (immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motif—a phosphatase-docking site, not an ITAM), recruits the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2, an enzyme that strips phosphates off other proteins.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: Contrast where and how CTLA-4 and PD-1 brake T-cell activation.
cards.back: CTLA-4 brakes outside by outbidding CD28 for B7 and stripping B7; PD-1 brakes inside by recruiting the phosphatase SHP-2 to strip activating phosphates off signalling proteins.
cards.why: In a rebuilt membrane system, SHP-2 reached CD28 most readily, and T-cell work suggests the antigen-receptor pathway is damped as well.
cards.quote: The second film traced how signal two licenses activation and how two brakes act outside or inside the membrane
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: Suppose a mutation replaces the main tyrosine in PD-1's cytoplasmic ITSM with a residue that cannot be phosphorylated. What happens when this activated T cell encounters a PD-L1-displaying tumour cell, and why?
cards.back: The PD-1 brake fails and T-cell signalling continues, because without ITSM phosphorylation PD-1 cannot recruit the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2 to remove activating phosphates.
cards.quote: Two tyrosines on PD-1's tail are phosphorylated when PD-L1 binds; the main one, in the ITSM
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: A naive T cell encounters a self peptide on a healthy tissue cell displaying neither B7 nor PD-L1, and later encounters the same peptide on an infected presenting cell displaying abundant B7. Predict the T cell's response at the second encounter, and explain how this safeguard differs from PD-1.
cards.back: The T cell remains unresponsive (anergic) during the second encounter; unlike PD-1, which is displayed on already-activated T cells to brake signalling inside the membrane when PD-L1 is present, anergy silences naive T cells before activation. This rests on the rules that signal one without CD28–B7 co-stimulation drives a naive T cell into lasting anergy, while PD-1 brakes activated T cells upon binding PD-L1.
cards.quote: In the classic experiments on cultured T cells, signal one alone did worse than nothing: the cells entered a lasting unresponsive state called anergy.
cards.section: One signal is not enough: the second signal and two brakes

cards.front: How do checkpoint-blocking antibodies against CTLA-4 or PD-1 limit tumour growth without ever binding to tumour cells?
cards.back: They cover the inhibitory receptor on the patient's own T cells, releasing the brake so stalled T cells that recognise altered tumour proteins keep running.
cards.quote: Antibodies covering a brake act on the patient's own T cells, never touching the tumour, so a stalled response runs on.
cards.section: Releasing a brake to treat cancer

cards.front: Suppose mice carrying PD-L1-displaying tumours have their T cells removed before receiving an anti-PD-1 blocking antibody. Predict the effect on tumour growth, and explain why.
cards.back: The antibody will not hold the tumours back, because checkpoint-blocking antibodies never attack the tumour directly—they work only by releasing the brake on T cells that recognise the tumour.
cards.quote: Antibodies covering a brake act on the patient's own T cells, never touching the tumour, so a stalled response runs on.
cards.section: Releasing a brake to treat cancer

cards.front: Knockout mice lacking CTLA-4 die within weeks from unchecked lymphocyte proliferation, whereas mice lacking PD-1 develop milder, later lupus-like autoimmunity. What clinical side effects follow checkpoint blockade, and which target triggers them more often?
cards.back: Autoimmune inflammation of organs such as the gut, skin, liver, and hormone glands occurs, and—as the knockout phenotypes predict—is generally more common with CTLA-4 blockade than with PD-1 blockade.
cards.quote: Autoimmune inflammation of the gut, skin, liver and hormone glands—and, as the knockouts predicted, generally more common with CTLA-4 blockade than with PD-1 blockade.
cards.section: Releasing a brake to treat cancer

cards.front: A tumour displays altered peptides on MHC, lacks PD-L1, and sits in a patient whose tumour-recognising T cells are held back by CTLA-4 outcompeting CD28 for B7. Predict the relative effectiveness of anti-PD-1 versus anti-CTLA-4 blockade, and state the expected clinical trade-off.
cards.back: Anti-CTLA-4 should unleash the T-cell response whereas anti-PD-1 should have little effect because no PD-L1 is engaging PD-1, with the trade-off of generally more common autoimmune inflammation of organs such as gut, skin, liver, and hormone glands. This rests on the rules that anti-PD-1 works by preventing PD-1 from meeting PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4 restores CD28 access to B7, and CTLA-4 blockade triggers autoimmune inflammation more often than PD-1 blockade.
cards.quote: In mice, blocking CTLA-4 caused tumour rejection (Dana Leach, Krummel and Allison, 1996), and preventing PD-1 from meeting PD-L1 held tumours back
cards.section: Releasing a brake to treat cancer

cards.front: Why does a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell recognise its target without requiring peptide presentation on an MHC protein?
cards.back: Its outer domain is a single-chain antibody fragment, which grips a folded surface protein directly rather than a peptide in an MHC groove.
cards.quote: Because an antibody grips a folded surface protein directly, the hybrid needs no peptide or MHC.
cards.section: Building a receptor from parts

cards.front: A patient receives engineered CAR T cells whose receptor links an outer antibody fragment to only the cytoplasmic zeta tail (three ITAMs). Predict how these cells perform in a dish versus in the patient, and state what design change fixes the problem.
cards.back: They kill target cells in a dish but often fail to multiply and persist in patients, because zeta alone supplies signal one without signal two; adding a CD28 or 4-1BB cytoplasmic domain to the same chain supplies both signals.
cards.quote: Early zeta-only CAR T cells killed targets in a dish yet often failed to multiply and persist in patients (signal one without signal two).
cards.section: Building a receptor from parts

cards.front: Name the two major clinical hazards that follow directly from the wiring of CAR T cells.
cards.back: On-target attack on healthy cells displaying the same surface protein, and severe whole-body cytokine inflammation when many CAR T cells fire together and macrophages multiply their cytokines.
cards.quote: When many CAR T cells fire at once, their cytokines—multiplied by the patient's own macrophages—can severely inflame the whole body.
cards.section: Building a receptor from parts

cards.front: CD19-directed CAR T cells destroy normal B cells alongside CD19-positive leukaemia cells. What deficit does this cause, and why is targeting a protein also expressed on lung-lining cells far more dangerous?
cards.back: Losing normal B cells removes antibody production, which can be managed with supplied antibodies, whereas on-target killing of vital lung-lining cells cannot be replaced that way and is far more life-threatening.
cards.quote: Because normal B cells also display CD19, the treatment removes them and patients may need supplied antibodies.
cards.section: Building a receptor from parts

cards.front: Suppose a tumour stops displaying MHC proteins on its surface yet still displays a folded tumour surface protein and PD-L1. Compare whether anti-PD-1 checkpoint blockade or a second-generation CAR targeting that surface protein can enable T cells to kill the tumour.
cards.back: The CAR T cell can kill the tumour, whereas anti-PD-1 blockade will fail. This rests on the rules that native T-cell receptors recognise peptides in an MHC groove—and checkpoint blockade helps only when the patient already has T cells recognising the tumour—whereas a CAR's antibody fragment grips a folded surface protein directly without needing peptide or MHC.
cards.quote: Because an antibody grips a folded surface protein directly, the hybrid needs no peptide or MHC.
cards.section: Building a receptor from parts

cards.front: Design a single-chain CAR against a tumour displaying surface protein Marker-X (also found at low levels on lung-lining cells): assign modular parts for recognition, signal one, and signal two, and predict two resulting harms.
cards.back: Use anti-Marker-X antibody variable regions with a linker, hinge, and transmembrane segment for recognition, the zeta tail's three ITAMs for signal one, and a CD28 or 4-1BB cytoplasmic domain for signal two; harms are life-threatening on-target killing of Marker-X lung-lining cells and macrophage-amplified whole-body cytokine inflammation. This rests on the rules that antibodies bind folded surface proteins directly, CAR persistence requires both ITAMs and co-stimulation, and CARs attack any healthy cell carrying the same target.
cards.quote: Using parts from an antibody, the T-cell receptor complex and a co-stimulatory receptor, assign recognition, signal one and signal two
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why did sequencing the T-cell receptor take years, and what did Chien and Davis discover once the receptor chain gene was cloned?
cards.back: T cells keep the receptor membrane-bound and release none of it; cloning showed the receptor gene is cut and rejoined in T cells, as antibody genes are in B cells.
cards.quote: showed the gene is cut and rejoined in T cells, as antibody genes are in B cells (the white blood cells that make antibodies).
cards.section: Cloning the T-cell receptor and the B-cell parallel

cards.front: How does the B-cell receptor follow the same partner-ITAM signalling plan as the T-cell receptor?
cards.back: A membrane-bound antibody with a three-amino-acid tail (in its IgM form) pairs with Ig-alpha and Ig-beta (one ITAM each), phosphorylated mainly by Lyn and read by Syk.
cards.quote: The B-cell receptor follows the same partner-ITAM plan: a membrane-bound antibody with a three-amino-acid tail (in its IgM form), flanked by Ig-alpha and Ig-beta carrying one ITAM each.
cards.section: Cloning the T-cell receptor and the B-cell parallel

cards.front: Suppose a T cell carries a loss-of-function mutation in the membrane scaffold LAT. Compare the expected impact on activation through its native T-cell receptor versus through an engineered CAR.
cards.back: Activation through the native T-cell receptor should fail because the calcium–NFAT, PKC–NF-κB, and Ras–AP-1 branches all leave LAT, whereas CAR activation should be less impaired. This rests on the rules that ZAP-70 phosphorylates LAT as the docking scaffold launching all three native TCR pathways, while a CAR's intracellular signals depend less on LAT.
cards.quote: Finally, a CAR's intracellular signals are not identical to the native T-cell receptor's and depend less on LAT.
cards.section: Lck association, PD-1 targets, checkpoint nuances and CAR signalling
